name: The golden-window conjecture
title: The golden-window conjecture | Takuya Nemoto
description: A conjecture on a three-player repeated game, and its proof: for discount factors in the window from 1/φ to 2/3, the payoffs that can be kept without randomization form a set of length zero, whose dimension is the root of an equation in δ. Both parts were resolved on 18 November 2026. Part (a) and the formula of part (b) are special cases of known theorems; continuity and strict increase in δ and the limits at both ends were not found in the texts read.
taglineHtml: This page is about a conjecture on one segment of payoffs in one three-player game, and its proof. Proved: what happens below the window, at its lower end and from 2/3 up, and, inside the window, that the set has positive dimension, that it has length zero, and how its dimension behaves. The proofs of the last two were written on 18 November 2026. Length zero and the dimension formula are special cases of known theorems; the behaviour of the dimension along this game’s curve was not found in the texts read.

blocks.title: Where it stands
blocks.html:
The golden-window conjecture has two parts. Both are proved: part (a) is Proposition 8 and part (b) is Proposition 9 of the note. Status: resolved (part (a) and the formula of part (b) are special cases of known theorems; continuity and strict increase in δ and the limits at both ends were not found in the texts read). The name stays as the name of the problem, because it is already in published DOIs and in issue labels. The conjecture was stated in a note that applies the operator of the three Trinity-Infinity papers to a repeated game (trinity-operator, games). An English paper version, with Propositions 1–7 and the conjecture, is on Figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.34419198, 13 October 2026). It is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed. The posted version is frozen, and it still states both parts as conjectures. Corrections go into the note. Propositions 8 and 9 are in the note and in the resolution paper, a separate Figshare item (10.6084/m9.figshare.35050300). The resolution paper is not a new version of the posted one. Its DOI was received on 18 November 2026.

Propositions 8 and 9. The proofs were written by Claude Code (Anthropic) at the author’s request on 18 November 2026. The author is responsible for them. The literature was checked on the same day. Proposition 8 is known: it is an immediate special case of Lu, Steiner and Zou (2026), Proposition 2.5, and it is counted as zero. The formula of Proposition 9 is a special case of their Theorem 1.2 with Lemma 2.7, and that part is zero. Continuity along this curve, where the base and the hole move together, strict increase in δ and the limits at both ends were not found in the texts read, and are not yet counted.

The question. Three players each choose to cooperate or defect. With k co-players cooperating, a cooperator gets k + 1 and a defector k + 2, the payoff table of Series I. The game is repeated without end, with discount factor δ. Which payoffs (2+t, 4−t, 2+t), with 0 < t ≤ 1, can be kept as an equilibrium without randomization? Call that set of t the set T_δ. The end (2,4,2), which Series II called sustainable, cannot be kept for any δ (Proposition 3).

δ < 1/2No t can be kept. Proved (Proposition 4).

1/2 ≤ δ < 1/φOnly t = δ and t = 1. Proved (Proposition 5).

δ = 1/φA countably infinite set. Proved (Proposition 5).

1/φ < δ < 2/3, the windowPositive Hausdorff dimension: proved (Proposition 6). (a) Length zero: proved (Proposition 8), a special case of known theorems. (b) Dimension below 1, continuous and strictly increasing in δ, tending to 0 at the lower end and to 1 at the upper end: proved (Proposition 9); the formula is a special case of known theorems. The dimension is the root of an equation in δ. Strictly increasing is stronger than the conjecture’s non-decreasing. Before the proofs, the evidence was numerical: refined period by period, the total length of the surviving intervals kept shrinking, and the dimension estimate grew with δ.

δ ≥ 2/3Every t from 1 − δ to 1. Proved (Proposition 5).

With public randomizationt can be kept exactly when δ ≥ max(1/2, 1 − t). Proved (Proposition 4).

blocks.title: Move δ
blocks.html: The figure is drawn in the browser from the recursion of Propositions 5 and 6. It fetches nothing. The upper band is the discount factor, with the window marked. The lower band shows the values of t that survive a finite number of periods. That is numerical evidence, not a proof.

blocks.title: What is claimed, and on what conditions
blocks.html:
This is not a theory. The proofs have not been checked against the literature, and no third party has recognised them. Under those conditions, three contributions are claimed. The propositions are a contribution as mathematical proof, which moves to zero if an earlier statement is found. The conjecture is the contribution of posing a question. Its answer, Propositions 8 and 9, is counted with the propositions. The route of rediscovery is a case study in the philosophy of science (Machine-mediated Rediscovery, SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.7537983), which passed SSRN’s screening and has not been peer-reviewed. Claiming a contribution and having the field count it are different things.

The contribution of the three papers to mathematics is zero. The proofs outside the window are not zero: they are not yet counted. The same holds for Propositions 6 and 9 inside it. Proposition 8 and the formula of Proposition 9 were checked and are zero: they are special cases of known theorems. Zero means the check was made and nothing new was found. Not yet counted means the check has not been made.

The mathematical significance is conditional on the literature check. If the same statements exist earlier, the significance belongs to that work. The significance for the philosophy of science stays as it was. A rediscovery that contributes nothing as a result can, when the model is pushed further, still lead to a question that has not been answered.

Proving it moves up only this one statement. The operator remains a special case of a known model, and the framework does not become a new theory.

Propositions 1–7 have not been checked against the literature. Berg and Kitti (2014) showed that pure-strategy equilibrium payoff sets can be fractals. Per their abstract, which is all that was read, they give a method to estimate the dimension. The papers’ operator is a special case of the Friedkin–Johnsen model.

The name describes the statement. It is not a person’s name. The window is the interval of discount factors from 1/φ to 2/3. Its lower end is also the threshold at which three players taking turns to defect becomes an equilibrium (Proposition 1). Both come from the polynomial δ² + δ − 1. Whether that is a coincidence is not known. It is kept as a question, not as a conjecture.

The conjecture, the proofs and the figure were written with Claude Code (Anthropic). The author is responsible for the claims. Claude is not an author.
